meta.title: Who really said "Loyalty to a company, it's nonsense"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Jack Welch really said it, to the Wall Street Journal on 4 August 1988. Quote sites cite a 2005 book instead and drop his qualifying second sentence.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Loyalty to a company, it's nonsense'?
meta.ogDescription: Jack Welch really said it — to the Wall Street Journal, 4 August 1988. The popular citation stops at a 2005 book and clips the sentence that followed.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Welch said it to Wall Street Journal reporter Janet Guyon for her front-page profile “Combative Chief: GE Chairman Welch, Though Much Praised, Starts to Draw Critics,” published 4 August 1988. Four independently reported books cite that article for this sentence, and one of them — Hedrick Smith’s Who Stole the American Dream? — carries an endnote keyed word-for-word to it.

source.excerpt: Loyalty to a company, it’s nonsense. If loyalty means that this company will ignore poor performance, then loyalty is off the table.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ carries the line in its Quotes section, but sources it only to Mark Ames’s Going Postal (2005), p. 98 — a book that is itself quoting the Wall Street Journal at second hand. Nearly every quote site online copies that dead end.

A full-text search across Internet Archive books ↗ finds the sentence in about nine distinct books, spread across roughly fifteen scanned editions. The earliest of them is Gary D. Kissler’s The Change Riders (Addison-Wesley, 1991), which already credits it to the Wall Street Journal — long before the 2005 book Wikiquote leans on.

Hedrick Smith’s Who Stole the American Dream? (Random House, 2012) ↗ closes the chain. Its endnote is keyed to this exact sentence and cites Janet Guyon, “Combative Chief: GE Chairman Welch, Though Much Praised, Starts to Draw Critics,” The Wall Street Journal, August 4, 1988. Smith and Greenhouse both punctuate the headline with a comma after “Combative Chief”; Kissler and the other citing books print the colon form used here.

Steven Greenhouse’s The Big Squeeze (Alfred A. Knopf, 2008) ↗ prints the fuller two-sentence version and cites the same Guyon article; Thomas F. O’Boyle’s At Any Cost and Christopher Byron’s Testosterone Inc. both cite it by the same date.
source.excerptNote: This is the fuller two-sentence form as printed by Steven Greenhouse in The Big Squeeze and Hedrick Smith in Who Stole the American Dream?, both of whom cite the 1988 Guyon article. Almost everywhere else online only the first sentence survives. The Journal’s 1988 archive is not publicly readable, so the two sentences are confirmed from those books rather than from the newsprint.

source.rightsNote: The sentence was first published in The Wall Street Journal on 4 August 1988, so the article carrying it is squarely in copyright in the United States — nothing published in 1931 or later has aged into the public domain. Welch’s spoken words reached print through Janet Guyon’s reporting, and the article remains behind the Journal’s paid archive. Quoting the line itself for comment and attribution is ordinary fair use; reproducing the article is not.

author.name: Jack Welch
author.heading: Who said it
author.metaLine: 1935–2020 · Chairman and CEO of General Electric, 1981–2001
author.bio: John Francis Welch Jr. ran General Electric from 1981 to 2001, a tenure that made him the most imitated executive of his era and, later, one of the most argued-over. He was nicknamed “Neutron Jack” in the early 1980s for shedding vast numbers of employees while the buildings stayed standing. His dismantling of the implicit lifetime-employment contract at GE — which he defended openly, in this quote and in interviews — is the part of his legacy that this sentence has come to stand for.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The attribution is sound — the failures here are in the citation chain and in the trimming, not in whether Welch said it.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ and the quote sites that copy it stop at this 2005 book, which is itself relaying the Wall Street Journal. The article behind it — named, dated and bylined in the endnotes of Smith and Greenhouse — almost never gets mentioned.

A question-mark form circulates widely, including in Reid Hoffman, Ben Casnocha and Chris Yeh’s The Alliance. Every book that cites the 1988 article prints the comma form instead — Kissler, Ames, O’Boyle, Byron, Greenhouse and Smith all do. Read the snippets in that full-text search ↗ rather than its hit count: the Internet Archive index ignores the punctuation, so the comma query and the question-mark query return the identical set of books.

Quoted alone it reads as contempt for loyalty as such. Greenhouse ↗ and Smith both print what followed — that if loyalty means ignoring poor performance, then loyalty is off the table — which is a narrower claim than the fragment implies.

misattribution.truthLine: Real speaker, real newspaper, real date: the endnote trail ↗ lands on Janet Guyon’s Wall Street Journal profile of 4 August 1988. For a name this heavily targeted by fabricated quotes, that is the unusual outcome.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: By August 1988 Welch had been running General Electric for seven years and had already earned the nickname “Neutron Jack” — a reference to the neutron bomb, for eliminating employees while leaving the buildings intact ↗. Guyon’s profile caught him at the moment the admiration was starting to curdle into criticism, and the loyalty line is the sentence that stuck.

Welch was not improvising a slogan. In a September–October 1989 Harvard Business Review interview ↗ he set out the same position at length: GE’s old implicit contract had produced what he called a paternal, feudal kind of loyalty that “tends to focus people inward,” and he wanted it replaced. The one-liner given to the Journal is the compressed version of a view he defended on the record.
context.detailsSummary: Why the citation chain is worth fixing
detailsBody: A quote can be perfectly genuine and still be badly sourced. This one has spent decades travelling with a citation that points at a 2005 book rather than the 1988 newspaper article, which makes it look thinner than it is — and leaves it indistinguishable, at a glance, from the invented lines that cluster around famous executives.

The correction is small and checkable: Janet Guyon, “Combative Chief: GE Chairman Welch, Though Much Praised, Starts to Draw Critics,” The Wall Street Journal, 4 August 1988 — the citation printed in the endnotes of Smith (2012) and Greenhouse (2008). O’Boyle (1998) and Byron cite the sentence to the Journal on that same date without naming the piece or its reporter, and the line was already appearing in print, credited to the Journal, as early as 1991.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Jack Welch page lists "Loyalty to a company, it's nonsense" in its Quotes section, sourced to: Originally said to the Wall Street Journal, quoted by Mark Ames in Going Postal (2005), p. 98.

The Harvard Business Review interview of September–October 1989, by Noel Tichy and Ram Charan, contains Welch saying GE's old paternal loyalty "tends to focus people inward" and redefining loyalty as an affinity among people who want to grapple with the outside world and win. It does NOT contain "Loyalty to a company, it's nonsense."

An Internet Archive full-text search for the exact phrase returns 15 books, including Gary D. Kissler's The Change Riders (which credits it to the Wall Street Journal), Thomas F. O'Boyle's At Any Cost, Christopher Byron's Testosterone Inc., Steven Greenhouse's The Big Squeeze, Hedrick Smith's Who Stole the American Dream?, Mark Ames's Going Postal, and The Alliance by Hoffman, Casnocha and Yeh (which prints the question-mark variant).

Hedrick Smith's Who Stole the American Dream? (Random House, 2012) contains the quote and an endnote keyed to it reading: "Loyalty to a company, it's nonsense" — Janet Guyon, "Combative Chief, GE Chairman Welch, Though Much Prized, Starts to Draw Critics," The Wall Street Journal, August 4, 1988. Internet Archive catalogue metadata confirms author Smith, Hedrick; date 2012; publisher New York: Random House.

Steven Greenhouse's The Big Squeeze (Alfred A. Knopf, 2008) contains both sentences — "Loyalty to a company, it's nonsense" and "If loyalty means that this company will ignore poor performance, then loyalty is off the table" — and cites Janet Guyon, "Combative Chief, GE Chairman Welch, Though Much Praised, Starts to Draw Critics," Wall Street Journal, in its notes. Internet Archive catalogue metadata confirms author Greenhouse, Steven; date 2008; publisher New York: Alfred A. Knopf.

Mark Ames's Going Postal (2005) contains the sentence "Loyalty to a company, it's nonsense," he told the Wall Street Journal. Internet Archive catalogue metadata confirms creator Mark Ames, date 2005.

Gary D. Kissler's The Change Riders was first published in 1991 by Addison-Wesley, and the Internet Archive holds a copy (identifier changeridersmana00kiss); its text contains "...Street journal as saying, 'Loyalty to a company, it's nonsense'".

Jack Welch was John Francis Welch Jr., born 19 November 1935, died 1 March 2020; he was chairman and CEO of General Electric 1981–2001; during the early 1980s he was dubbed "Neutron Jack" (in reference to the neutron bomb) for eliminating employees while leaving buildings intact.
